newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Rivals envy global expansion of S.Korea's Daewoo.
newsitem.headline: Rivals envy global expansion of S.Korea's Daewoo.

text.p: Aggressive global expansion efforts by South Korea's Daewoo Group are already showing tangible results and earning praise from the unlikeliest corners, corporate rivals and analysts said on Monday.
"Daewoo has moved very, very swiftly. At the same time the group's strategy seems to be well-focused," said an executive at the Hyundai Group.
"No other group in the country has bolder overseas investment plans than Daewoo. The group's expansion looks even threatening," said a Samsung Group spokesman.
Neither executive would allow his name to be used, an indication of the reluctance of South Korean companies to praise each other.
Daewoo, South Korea's fourth-largest conglomerate, said it would have $15 billion in overseas projects by 2000, employing 250,000 workers in more than 1,000 sites world wide.
By 2000, it said, it would be producing 20 million televisions world wide and 2.5 million vehicles annually in more than 10 countries, as well as building 30 hotels in 20 countries.
"Daewoo's sales will grow to $177 billion in 2000 from $68 billion in 1996, with more than 50 percent earned from overseas business," said Daewoo Group spokesman Lee Jung-seung.
Daewoo has announced plans to set up 20 entities around the world that will operate independently of Seoul headquarters to strengthen the group's operations abroad.
Analysts hailed Daewoo's globalisation, aimed at by-passing trade barriers and moving beyond the home market.

"Other Korean groups may well follow in Daewoo's footsteps to survive and grow. Daewoo's globalisation couldn't be more timely, given the receding domestic economy," said Vince Kim, an analyst at Jardine Flemming Securities.

Daewoo has emerged as the largest carmaker in Poland, Uzbekistan and Romania. The group expects to sell 500,000 vehicles in eastern Europe and the Commonwealth of Independent States this year, up from almost nothing in 1996.

It is the largest single foreign investor in Vietnam, where it is building hotels and producing electronics, vehicles and auto parts, the company said. It is also the telecommunications equipment supplier in Ukraine, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan.
"Daewoo appears to be welcomed in those countries because of its commitment to their industrial development," said Yang Dong-ki, analyst at Dongbang Peregrine Securities.
Daewoo officials have said the group is not interested in making a short-term profit, preferring to re-invest in its host nations for long-term gains.

Analysts said Daewoo's initiative in emerging markets, despite suspicion over red tape, political uncertainty and delays of market reforms, must have impressed the host nations, which in turn have granted Daewoo preferential treatment.
"Behind all success stories there is a hero, and Daewoo's hero is group chairman Kim Woo-choong, who spends about three quarters of a year abroad," said the Samsung official.
The indefatigable tycoon has earned a reputation for turning troubled companies around, as illustrated by Daewoo's success with its shipbuilding and car making units.

Kim said in a recent interview with Reuters that he had developed his own know-how in succeeding in emerging markets. "The key to success is building trust with the host nations and convincing them of co-prosperity," Kim said.
He dismissed the risks of unbridled expansion: "What risk? People have criticised Daewoo's weak finances. But sorry, our financial status is now much better than that of our rivals."
The Fair Trade Commission reported earlier this month that Daewoo's capital-to-asset ratio was 24.1 percent at the end of 1996, compared with 17.9 percent for Samsung and Hyundai.
